title: The First Civilisations · Episode 2
chapters: Ancient China and the first emperor

units.t: The First Civilisations. Episode two.
In this episode: The Indus Valley civilisation, Ancient China and the first emperor, Persia: the first superpower and The Maya, Aztecs and Inca.
Part one. The Indus Valley civilisation.
Five thousand years ago, cities in modern Pakistan and India had grid streets and covered drains.
We still can't read their writing.
A forgotten civilisation.
Along the Indus River and its neighbours, in today's Pakistan and north-west India, a major civilisation arose around the same time as Egypt's pyramids.
It is also called the Harappan civilisation, after Harappa, the first site excavated.
It was forgotten for thousands of years until archaeologists recognised it in the 1920s, at Harappa and Mohenjo-daro.
At its height it covered a larger area than Egypt or Mesopotamia, with more than a thousand known settlements, from small villages to big cities such as Dholavira and Rakhigarhi.
Population estimates vary widely, but some scholars suggest several million people at its peak.
Planned cities, clean water.
Mohenjo-daro and Harappa had streets in a rough grid, with wide main roads and smaller lanes.
Bricks came in consistent proportions, roughly 1:2:4 for thickness, width and length, across hundreds of kilometres.
That suggests shared rules.
Many cities had a raised citadel with public buildings above a lower residential town.
Mohenjo-daro's Great Bath, about 12 metres long, was sealed with bitumen.
The water engineering was remarkable.
Mohenjo-daro may have had hundreds of brick-lined wells.
Many houses had bathing areas and toilets draining into covered brick sewers with inspection holes.
Dholavira, in a drier area, built large reservoirs for rainwater.
Few places had anything comparable for thousands of years.
Farmers, crafts and trade.
Most Indus people were farmers and herders, growing wheat, barley, peas and sesame.
They were among the earliest to grow cotton and weave it into cloth.
Craftspeople drilled long, polished carnelian beads, so prized that similar ones turn up in Mesopotamian royal tombs.
They also made painted pottery, copper and bronze tools, and clay toys.
Merchants traded cotton, beads, gems and timber by land and along the Arabian coast.
Mesopotamian texts mention a land called Meluhha, probably the Indus region.
Standardised cube-shaped stone weights, following a consistent system, suggest organised trade.
The port of Lothal had a large brick basin that many think was a dockyard.
Seals and a silent script.
Thousands of small square seals, often showing bulls, elephants or a one-horned beast, were probably pressed into clay to mark goods and their owners.
The one-horned animal, sometimes called a unicorn, is the most common image, and its meaning is unknown.
The seals carry short inscriptions.
Several thousand inscribed objects survive, using around 400 different signs, but most inscriptions are only about five signs long.
There is no long text and no bilingual inscription to act as a key, as the Rosetta Stone did for Egyptian.
Many decipherments have been proposed, but scholars accept none.
Most agree it was usually written right to left.
Until it is read, we don't know their language or any names.
Rulers and decline.
Unlike Egypt and Mesopotamia, Indus sites show no obvious palaces, grand royal tombs or monuments glorifying rulers.
A small stone bust nicknamed the 'Priest-King' may not show a king at all.
The gap between rich and poor seems smaller than elsewhere, and there are few signs of large-scale warfare.
Some scholars suggest power was shared, though absence of evidence isn't evidence of absence.
Over a few centuries, the big cities were gradually abandoned as people moved to smaller villages, especially eastward.
Leading explanations include a weakening monsoon, shifting rivers and less trade with Mesopotamia.
The old idea of a sudden invasion is no longer widely accepted.
Mohenjo-daro is now a UNESCO World Heritage site, threatened by salt and erosion.
The key idea: The Indus civilisation was as old as Egypt's pyramids and larger in area, yet it was forgotten until the 1920s.
Part two. Ancient China and the first emperor.
One ruler united China, standardised its writing, linked its first great walls and was buried with an army of clay soldiers.
Dynasties and the Mandate.
Chinese civilisation grew along the Yellow and Yangtze rivers, where people farmed millet and rice.
The Shang dynasty, about 1600–1046 BC, left the earliest known Chinese writing, on oracle bones: priests carved questions to ancestors onto bones and shells, heated them and read the cracks.
The Shang were also masters of bronze casting.
The Zhou dynasty that overthrew them introduced the Mandate of Heaven: the idea that heaven grants the right to rule to a just ruler and withdraws it from a bad one.
Floods, famines and revolts could be read as signs a dynasty had lost the mandate, which justified rebellion.
The Warring States.
As Zhou power faded, China split into competing states, and by the end seven major powers were fighting for survival.
Constant war drove new ideas in the age of the Hundred Schools of Thought.
Confucius, who lived slightly earlier, taught respect, duty, family loyalty and government by virtuous example.
Daoism, traditionally traced to the possibly legendary Laozi, emphasised harmony with nature.
Legalists argued that strict laws, rewards and harsh punishments made a state strong.
Military thinking flourished too, including The Art of War, traditionally credited to Sun Tzu.
Iron tools and crossbows also changed farming and warfare.
The First Emperor.
King Ying Zheng of Qin, using Legalist ideas and a ruthless army, conquered the other states and declared himself Qin Shi Huang, 'First Emperor of Qin'.
The name China likely comes from Qin.
He replaced hereditary lords with officials appointed and paid by the centre, a system later dynasties kept.
He was also brutal: according to the historian Sima Qian, writing about a century later, he ordered books burned and scholars executed, though some details may be exaggerated.
To bind the empire together, he imposed one script, one currency and standard weights and measures.
He even fixed cart axle widths so wagons could use the same ruts.
Roads and canals moved troops and goods quickly.
He died in 210 BC, and his dynasty collapsed within four years.
Walls and clay soldiers.
Several Warring States had built walls against rivals and northern nomads.
Qin Shi Huang joined and extended the northern ones, using rammed earth and forced labour.
Most of the stone and brick wall tourists visit dates from the Ming dynasty, over 1,500 years later.
All its branches together stretch more than 20,000 kilometres.
It is not visible from the Moon with the naked eye, a popular myth.
In 1974, farmers digging a well near Xi'an found the Terracotta Army: an estimated 8,000 life-size soldiers, with horses and chariots, guarding the emperor in the afterlife.
Each face looks individual, and they were once brightly painted.
The emperor's own burial mound has never been opened.
Sima Qian described rivers of mercury inside, and soil tests have found unusually high mercury levels there.
Han: trade and inventions.
The Han dynasty kept Qin's centralised system but softened it, adopting Confucian ideas and choosing officials partly by recommendation and examination rather than birth alone.
That grew into the imperial civil service examinations, used for over a thousand years.
The emperor system lasted until 1912.
Around 138 BC, the envoy Zhang Qian travelled deep into Central Asia, and his reports helped open trade routes later called the Silk Road.
Silk, spices, horses, glass, ideas and religions moved along them, and Buddhism reached China from India this way.
Han China also developed paper, which Cai Lun improved around AD 105, and early lodestone direction-finders, ancestors of the compass.
China's majority ethnic group still calls itself the Han.
The key idea: The Shang left China's earliest writing, and the Zhou introduced the Mandate of Heaven, which justified rebellion against bad rulers.
Part three. Persia: the first superpower.
Long before Rome, a Persian king built an empire stretching from Egypt to India.
The Achaemenid Persians ran it with roads, couriers, coins and a surprising degree of tolerance.
Cyrus and his Cylinder.
Around 550 BC, Cyrus of Persis, in south-western Iran, overthrew the Median kingdom that had dominated his people.
Within about twenty years he conquered Lydia in Asia Minor and in 539 BC Babylon.
His dynasty is the Achaemenids.
His son Cambyses added Egypt, and Darius pushed east into the Indus Valley and west into Europe.
At its height it covered more land than any empire before it.
The Cyrus Cylinder, a 23-centimetre clay barrel found at Babylon in 1879, records that Cyrus restored temples and let displaced peoples return home.
The Hebrew Bible also praises him for letting Jewish exiles rebuild their temple.
Calling it the first human rights charter goes too far: it is royal propaganda.
But it reflects a real policy of working with local customs.
Darius organises an empire.
Darius I, who ruled from 522 to 486 BC, was the great organiser.
He divided the empire into provinces called satrapies, each run by a governor known as a satrap.
Satraps collected taxes and kept order, but the king also sent inspectors, whom the Greeks nicknamed 'the eyes and ears of the king', to check on them.
Darius introduced a gold coin, the daric, and standardised weights and measures.
Officials often wrote in Aramaic, which became a common administrative language across the Near East.
Darius also recorded his rise to power on a huge rock carving at Behistun in western Iran, in three languages.
Centuries later it helped scholars such as Henry Rawlinson crack cuneiform.
Royal Road and Persepolis.
To hold the realm together, the Persians needed fast communication.
The Royal Road ran roughly 2,500 kilometres from Sardis, near the Aegean, to Susa.
Stations along it gave official messengers fresh horses, food and rest.
Herodotus wrote that nothing, not snow, rain, heat or darkness, stopped these couriers.
A version of his words is carved on New York City's main post office.
A journey of three months on foot could reportedly be relayed in about a week.
At Persepolis, Darius built a palace complex whose Apadana hall had tall stone columns topped with carved animals.
Carvings show delegates from across the empire bringing gifts, each in their own clothing.
Rather than slaughter, the art shows peaceful order, many peoples under one ruler.
Faith and fire.
Many Persian kings honoured Ahura Mazda, the wise lord at the centre of Zoroastrianism, one of the world's oldest surviving religions.
Its prophet, Zarathustra, known to the Greeks as Zoroaster, taught of a struggle between truth and order on one side and the lie and chaos on the other.
Darius's inscriptions repeatedly attack 'the Lie' and present the king as its enemy.
Fire was a sacred symbol of purity, a tradition still important in Zoroastrian fire temples today.
Scholars debate how the kings' beliefs related to later Zoroastrian practice.
Some ideas, such as a final judgement and a struggle between good and evil, may have influenced later religions, though that too is debated.
Greek wars and the end.
Much of what Westerners learned about Persia came from its enemies.
Darius and his son Xerxes invaded Greece in 490 and 480 BC and were defeated at battles such as Marathon and Salamis.
Greek writers portrayed the Persians as luxurious and tyrannical, a picture that coloured European views for centuries.
In reality, Persia remained a great power for another 150 years.
Its end came when Alexander the Great defeated Darius III in a series of battles and took the empire.
In 330 BC Persepolis was burned, whether by accident, revenge or celebration is still argued.
Yet Alexander adopted many Persian ways of ruling, and later Iranian empires, the Parthians and Sasanians, would rise again.
The key idea: Cyrus built a vast empire in one lifetime and presented himself as a liberator, a policy of working with local customs.
Part four. The Maya, Aztecs and Inca.
Pyramids, floating gardens and a road network across the Andes.
The Americas produced great civilisations with no contact with Europe or Asia.
Civilisations of the Americas.
People reached the Americas at least 15,000 years ago, most likely from Asia.
Without contact with Eurasia, they domesticated crops that now feed the world: maize, potatoes, tomatoes, cacao, chillies, squash and many beans.
In Mesoamerica, modern Mexico and Central America, and the Andes, complex societies arose with cities, monumental architecture and states.
The Olmecs, from around 1200 BC, are often called Mesoamerica's first civilisation, famous for colossal carved stone heads.
In the Andes, Caral in Peru was building large ceremonial mounds nearly 5,000 years ago, around the time of Egypt's early pyramids.
The Maya.
The Maya flourished especially between about AD 250 and 900, in city-states such as Tikal, Palenque and Copán.
They were never one empire: rival kingdoms formed alliances and fought wars.
Kings recorded their deeds on carved stone stelae.
Their writing, using several hundred glyphs, was the most complete in the ancient Americas, and scholars have largely deciphered it since the 1970s and 1980s.
Maya mathematics counted in base 20 using a dot for one, a bar for five and a shell for zero.
They were among the few ancient peoples to develop zero independently.
Priests tracked the Sun, Moon and Venus and could predict eclipses.
Their Long Count calendar began at 3114 BC.
The 2012 'end of the world' was a modern myth: a cycle simply rolled over, like an odometer.
The Aztecs.
The Mexica, or Aztecs, founded Tenochtitlan on an island in Lake Texcoco around 1325.

It grew into one of the world's largest cities, with perhaps 200,000 people, connected to the shore by causeways and fed partly by chinampas: farm plots built up from the lake bed with mud and plants.
From 1428 the Aztecs led an alliance of three cities that conquered much of central Mexico, demanding regular tribute of maize, cloth, cacao, feathers and gold.
They practised human sacrifice on a large scale, believing it helped keep the Sun moving and the world in balance.
Modern Mexico City stands on the ruins.
The Inca.
In the 1400s, especially under Pachacuti, the Inca expanded from Cusco to an empire of about 4,000 kilometres, from modern Ecuador to Chile.
They built roughly 40,000 kilometres of roads with rope bridges, and relay runners called chasquis carried messages hundreds of kilometres in a day or two.
Their tight stonework at Machu Picchu and Cusco has survived major earthquakes.
The Inca had no written script as we know it.
Officials recorded numbers, and possibly more, on knotted cords called khipu, where knot type and position showed values in base 10.
Instead of money, people paid tax in labour, called mit'a, and the state stored food, cloth and weapons in storehouses.
Farmers built terraces and freeze-dried potatoes into chuño.
Conquest and legacy.
Hernán Cortés arrived in Mexico in 1519 with a few hundred Spaniards.
Allied with tens of thousands of Indigenous people who resented Aztec rule, he took Tenochtitlan in 1521.
Francisco Pizarro captured the Inca emperor Atahualpa in 1532, as a civil war split the empire.
The biggest killer was disease: smallpox and other illnesses, to which Indigenous Americans had no immunity, killed a huge share of the population.
These were not 'lost' civilisations.
Millions still speak Mayan languages, Nahuatl and Quechua.
English words like chocolate, tomato, avocado and chilli come from Nahuatl.
Potatoes transformed European diets, and Indigenous communities now lead efforts to protect their languages, sites and stories.
The key idea: Without any contact with Eurasia, Americans domesticated crops that now feed the world and built cities and states.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What was remarkable about the Indus civilisation's place in history?
Answer. As old as Egypt's pyramids but forgotten until the 1920s.
Question two. What was the Mandate of Heaven?
Answer. The idea that heaven grants rule to just rulers.
Question three. How do historians generally view the claim that the Cyrus Cylinder was the first human rights charter?
Answer. As an overstatement of what was royal propaganda.
Question four. What is notable about the crops the early Americans domesticated?
Answer. They arose independently and now feed the world.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
